Oh man, I love this girl!

After being expelled for assaulting a teacher at her Catholic school, Maria Kawai transfers to a public school that is also her last chance. Once there she runs into the same problem as at her old school with people misunderstanding her blunt tone for cruelness, thus leading the majority of the class to tease and taunt her, to the point even her own teacher automatically assumes Maria is always at fault. But the class king and bad boy are drawn to Maria and help her to make friends, be understood, and see the world with a lovely spin.

With this first volume I have to say, I absolutely love Maria! Her bluntness and awkward social skills remind me a bit of myself. What people mistake as cold and uncaring is actually Maria seeing through to their hearts and speaking out the ugly truth that they're hiding, from even themselves sometimes. That may sound rough on the surface, however I believe she does it as a way of protecting people from others harsh feelings, without realizing that is actually hurting the very people she is trying to protect.

The art is very pretty, it's classic shojo with sketchy sleek lines, and while most of the characters match said style, Maria has notably bigger eyes and drawn in more of moe style art.

This is a definite series for any romance fan to try out. I am really looking forward to seeing where the series goes, and I definitely want to see Maria end up with a certain bad boy.

I am loving this series!

As Maria's feelings for Shin start bubbling closer to the surface, Maria gets reunited with a former friend from her old school whose intentions for coming back into Maria's life are sketchy at best. Chaos inducing and heart breaking at worse.

I'm not one to pay close attention to tropes or genres, I like what I like, but high school love triangles are a bit done in my opinion. They're not necessarily a bad thing, they're so popular cause they do work and they are entertaining, however it is better when the triangle shifts into different shapes such as a square, or cube if you will.

I hope in this case it's more like a circle within the middle of an S, so the main couple stays together. Poor Yusuke, the boy is a total simp/manic-pixie-dream-boy, I wish he would gain more self-worth to see himself more than a helper.

And I wish Tomoyo and Ayu got more page time, I think it would be fun peeking into their lives a bit more.

I can't wait to read on!

No... No!!

I am huffing right now. For the past 2 volumes things have been getting more dramatic in odd ways, but ways that are on theme for the story and characters. However, this time, this volume has taken too far, and I will not stand for it!  I believe that blame should not be assigned unless that is the only way to see how to fix the problem, I am feeling feelings at the moment of writing this and I don't care, I blame the editor, Ms. K. Dead stop.

Now I will explain how; during this volume, Maria finally lets her feelings out and recall's memories of her troubling past, and the person who reveals their feelings to her, (I'm not saying who as to not spoil anything,) practically assaults her and gropes her even though that is completely out of his character right after she gets emotional and says it she wants to "give him something." Nowhere through the rest of the series has that particular lust came out so strongly nor so surprisingly. (Well, when Shintaro, aka Eros, came into the picture he was just as blunt as Maria was in the beginning, so he said something shocking, but he didn't mean anything by it.)

So why I am assigning blame to Ms. K is because Mr. O, the first editor for the series, left sometime around the end of volume 6, I am guessing on the timeline though as his departure was announced in volume 8, and in the afterward it said that while Ms. Kay is a very lovely lady who would bring pastry, she is also ruthless in her notes and said that parts needed to be more dramatic, and it seemed like around that volume things did become more dramatic, and even Maria seemed less like Maria. Not just because she was maturing as a person, something else felt different.

While my love of the characters and Maria has not waned, I do hope that the story comes a bit more back to its roots and shows our favorite heroine and her friends in a lovelier light.

Did I use this review to vent? Yes, yes I did.
Is that unusual for me? Yes, indeed it is. …

"She is the most beautiful devil."
4.5* stars

Six months after Shin's departure, Maria and company are making plans for their future as they venture into their senior year. Everyone has ideas or knows where they want to go in their life, but Maria is unsure where to go with her future. An unexpected visitor sets Maria on a path that everyone else saw coming, but devils need to find their own way to their dreams.

While I'm sad the series has come to an end, I believe this is a good ending for the characters, albeit everything was tied up a bit suddenly and cleanly to me.  There was a 6 month time jump in the beginning, which is probably why things seemed sudden, however things with Maria's biological father and her grandparents, (mother side,) all seemed too perfect.

Within the past 2 volumes everything fell into place just like that, the grandparents forgiving the man who assaulted their daughter (Anna, Maria's mom) when she was 14, was forgiven just because he couldn't sing Amazing Grace, cares deeply for Maria, and fell in love with their daughter while corresponding with her by letters. Shintaro being the foster son to said man, (who has turned his life around,) was one thing, but the sudden and utter forgiveness of the grandparents felt too unrealistic. Although it was kind of nice to see people forgive one another at face value, it was still a bit much.

I like that in this volume a couple of the chapters were in other characters point of view, especially the final chapter being in Yusuke's point of view, I feel like he was the best person to describe the ending and what it meant to Maria and the others. And while I did like all the characters, I do wish that more chapters centered around Ayu and Tomoyo instead of centering around the boys so much of the time. …

Predators have a bad name. He only wants love!

A simple, yet odd love story... A lonely polar bear falls in love with a Little seal that is terrified of its natural predator. Can their relationship last, or should it even begin?

I don't like talking about other opinions in my reviews, but I will say, I've heard about peoples worries that the aging of the animals is a little uncomfortable. The seal is quite young, and the polar bear is... not as young. Their specific ages are obviously not stated in the book, but Seal is quite young, he still has not learned how to swim and is reliant on his mother: Polar Bear has had a bit of trauma in his life and looks to be fully grown. However, given his emotional maturity, I would assume he would only be a teenager to early 20s at most if we're talking human years. Which yes, that would not be good with humans, but since animals age and mature differently, I don't see the same issues in that area as others have.

However, Polar Bear is very dense, and so so very lonely. He doesn't realize that he is technically holding Seal hostage, and I can't really tell if Seal is beginning to understand that Polar Bear means him no harm, or if it's the beginning of Stockholm Syndrome. That is more what I worry about. Their whole schtick is that Seal is afraid of Polar Bear, it's natural predator. Their feelings - particularly Polar Bear's - on the other hand don't normally play into the circle of life. So I really hope the future volumes play a bit less into the fear and more of understanding where the other is coming from.

All of that said, I do intend to continue reading as the story is inviting and the simple, yet tasteful art is adorable! Especially the bonus artwork in between the chapters. If you're looking for a laid back read, definitely check this book out. Even if you only want the first volume and treat it as a one shot, it is worth it.

A world as silent as falling snow.

For many, the world is just noise, but for Yuki - an everyday college student - the world is silent. Yuki has caring friends, gets good grades, and has always been deaf. She navigates the world by reading lips and communicating through writing on her phone and sign language. But a chance meeting with a white-haired polyglot, Itsuomi, sparks something new: the urge to widen her world. He also ignited something else within her... But is Itsuomi's only interested in learning about Yuki's world because she's never had a deaf friend, or is there more behind his love of learning other cultures?

Ohmagosh ohmagosh, this is so flipping adorable!! I absolutely loved everything about this volume Istuomi's expressions are priceless, and it was so cute when Yuki couldn't see what Itsuomi was thinking when it was pretty obvious. The vibe to me was very chill and lighthearted, it really matched the flowers on the cover. Not to get too poetic here, but it felt as if Cherry Blossoms were a story. I'm not sure how to describe it.

The art was pretty and sparkly, adding to the elegance of the volume. I loved the hand signs used to showcase sign language. At the beginning of a chapter, it was explained that the author has a consultant that helps with the sign language to make it as accurate as possible, as it is difficult to depict movements in still panels. Also, Japanese sign language differs from American sign language, just like spoken languages do, and it was really cool learning little fun facts like that relating to Yuki's world, and the real world.

I am so excited to read more of A Sign of Affection and look forward to seeing Istuomi and Yuki's relationship grow!

An eye for an eye only perpetuates, it's not a solution.

Shoya's Mission in life is to find a cure for boredom. He does this by being a daredevil and his class's worst bully. His friends put up with him because he's fun, but after a deaf transfer student, Shoko enters his class, he puts all of his energy into torturing her. Eventually, his bullying forces her to leave school, then the table turns and Shoya gets a taste of his own medicine. However, 6 years later, after Shoya understands the error in his ways, the two meet again, can he make up for his past sins, or is it too late?

As a homeschooled kid, I have no personal parameters of what school life is like. But as someone with a conscience, Shoya is a major bully and a slight part of me felt the retaliation he felt after Shoko's transfer out of his school was deserved, but just as he never let up on Shoko, his classmates didn't let up on him. It's one thing if he learned a lesson from the childish retribution, but instead, he was bullied with intensity, but for longer. No one deserves that, not even a bully.

The art was wonderful, it's a bit more realistic than general manga style, and along with the attention to detail, it really helped to pull me into the characters world and their emotions, which was also on point. Like the art, the story itself felt very realistic which made me feel even more for the characters, and want to know more about them, and if Shoya can redeem himself.

This was a great volume, and I believe it will be a fantastic series, one that I'm very looking forward to getting the following volumes so I can follow Shoya and Shoko's story.

I wish I was a secret agent in high school.

Mostly so I could be 16 again though, lol.

For such a young girl, Luna is a very good secret agent. And frankly, I can very much relate to being unprepared for teenage emotional issues. After all, who isn't, right... right?

crickets chirping in the background.

Ahem,  The story was very fun to read. The art was cute, but lacking some with scenery. It's reminiscent of Pokémon with the classical big anime eyes, but the overall art had a sharper edge that I believe appeals to a more mature audience too.

The story jumps into the action within the first few pages, but slows down a little bit by the middle for more setup and character development. It is definitely worth sticking around though, because it picks backup again and doesn't stop, including through the following volumes.

 You can feel the care that went into writing The Amazing Agent Luna leap off the page, or screen for some readers. The story is family friendly, something that an adult or a younger person would enjoy reading, so long as they're young at heart.

I'll be honest, I went into this thinking I would not like it as much as I did.

The story of humanity being sequestered inside walls from the outside world to protect them from humanoid like Titans, to the tale of how Eren and Mikasa lost their mother, by said Titans, after a new, larger Titan called Colossus Titan destroyed the wall that had saved humanity from the gigantic threats for over 100 years. Then five year later, Eren and Mikasa, along with their friend Armin, graduated at the top of their class giving them the choice to serve in the inter most wall as royal guards, join the Garrison and be the first line protectors of the remaining walls, or join the survey corps and explore the outside world while defeating Titans and keeping them at bay.

It pulled me in and left me wanting more.

However, my only beef would be that the Titans creep me out. I'm OK with the sometimes gruesome images of the Titans pulling people apart and eating them limb by limb, but the Titans themselves are disturbing to me. The main reason is how some, especially Colossus Titan, are depicted without skin, mostly on their facial features showing the underlying tendons and muscles. To be clear, while that discourage me from reading Attack on Titan in the first place, I do not believe it'll stop me from reading further.

While the first volume is mainly for the setup of the story, it already shows great potential to the characters for their evolution that is sure to shine through the rest of the volumes. The author does a beautiful job weaving the past and the present together seamlessly, in a way of how books transition from present to past through chapters, Hajime Isayama does so within each chapter of the manga making it feel as if I'm reading the dialogue of a novel while watching the scenes with brilliant illustrations.

The art matches the theme and overall feel of the story very well. …

As the characters were introduced it started off a little slow, layering mystery and clues on top of one another deepening the intrigue, and by chapter 3 things took off like a bullet. With a bullet.

It's a carnivore not-eat herbivore world out there

A murder mystery wrapped in a furry bow, that is how I would describe Beastars. However the mystery does takes a backseat to the everyday lives of the characters, which is not a bad thing since the character's lives are a bit of a mystery too lol.

It started off a little slow, yet right in the middle of the action with the intrigue that the 1st few pages present, it takes a very good author and story line to pull that off.  The world building is fabulous, and so interesting, the story doesn't just give two dimensional answers but digs deeper into of why the answers are what they are, also the questions are answered naturally by the characters or an easy to digest narrating bubbles so you don't get bogged down by lengthy explanations.

The similarities and contradictions of the character's personalities to their species is captivating to read. Take Legoshi for example, he's a grey wolf, a pack animal, he has strong loyalty to his friends and theater troop. But he is also a loner, afraid to get too close to anybody because he is large and his species is seen as scary, he does not want to accidentally hurt someone.

The art is lovely and perfect for the style and vibe of the series. It gives fantastic detail to the different animal characteristics of the characters to where it's easy to tell the difference between two characters apart that are the same species, besides just with clothes.

Beasters is definitely a manga I would recommend, and I look forward to checking out the anime on Netflix.

A great horror retelling of Beauty and the Beast.
4.5* stars.

After "witnessing" the murder of her mother by the dreaded Beast who steals beautiful women's faces, Belle was locked away for her supposed wretched appearance by her distraught papa. After years living locked away, without a kind word thrown at her, she escapes her attic of a jail cell when she hears the Beast has returned to their town and she wants answers about what truly happened to her mother. But when she finally confronts the "beast," another Beast appears and saves her. Why are there two beasts, and why did the one protect her? Including from her own father...

You want to root for Belle, but she is comes off really weak and self-loathing in the beginning, making it hard to cheer her on, but once she meets the male lead character, his forcefulness makes her speak up for herself, making her less whiny with the potential for a good amount of character growth.

All the characters personalities and their looks are interesting, the story is intriguing and engaging, and the pacing is spot on. The odd combination of horror and shojo art style is unique and enjoyable but takes a second to get used to.

Overall, a very good series that I am going to love immersing myself in Belle and Beast's world.

A beastly, yet beautiful retelling.

Can our favorite heroine Belle save the day, as what should be a joyous day for the country and a gruesome victory for La Mèdium. And will everyone really get what they want, or needed, out of their seeming triumph? A perilous battle ensues with devastating consequences and an ending that is very different than what anyone may think...

Somewhere in chapter 18, (out of 20,) the story felt much more rushed than the rest of the chapters, and the art lost its touch of elegance and seemed a tad basic, like a new (and I mean a new-to-the-craft,) artist joined the series.

I didn't feel the story was impacted too much by the change of art, especially as much by the sped-up pacing, but it did feel jarring and took me out of the world. I would like to note that the artist/author was having health issues according to the author notes, so I don't want to be too harsh about the abrupt changes in this volume. I am also very glad that they were able to finish the series.

With that out of the way, the entirety of this story was absolutely wonderful! It is one of best retellings I have read of a classic tale. The French words scattered throughout the dialogue was perfect and really set the mood for a fantastical romance, with a touch of horror. The characters "beastly"/other worldly forms match perfectly to their personalities, which the two cat maids pointed out comically in the ending skits of a volume.

The ending of this volume and the series was absolutely perfect and the meaning behind the ending was the true beauty in this series. Bravo!

So flipping cute!!

A lonely, nameless monster happens to meet a sweet blind girl, Lily, while on a walk through her forest. After overcoming the fear of being around humans and slowly coming to terms with her past, Lily opened her life to more than just the forest around her and even gave her a name: Heath.

I loved this story and wish that there were more volumes! Which, by the end there is a couple unresolved questions that doesn't impact the ending of the story much but does leave room for more volumes. It'd be great to learn more as the girl's relationship continues too. Heath and Lily are so sweet and good for each other.

The scenery is fleshed out well and fits perfectly for the vibe of the story, mellow and sweet. The art is well-defined, yet soft and airy. I loved Heath's character design, the combination of scales, furry ears, and a horn, it's a nice mismatch to make her physically "unattractive" as a beast, yet so cute, and beautiful on the inside.

While the pacing went a little fast at times, overall, everything was fantastic. Funny, sweet and a lot dramatic, a delicious triple threat.

Mysteries are buried deep within the mausoleum.
3 and 1/2 stars*

Dinah, morning death of her parents, is forced to move in with her aunt who believes she's mentally ill for seeing ghosts in their house. She sneaks out one night, against the orders of her aunt, and she and her friend Vincent stumble upon a hidden grove with a mausoleum full of the things Dinah dreads seeing; ghosts, and as a not so pleasant bonus, demons. One particular demon, Bali Lali (a cool looking demon,) reveals a contract with Dinah's signature (that she doesn't remember signing,) requiring her to clean out the ghosts that lingers in the vaults of the mausoleum. One. By. One. Or she dies.

After the beginning chapters of learning about the story's version of Massachusetts, the chapters became episodic, while still slightly building on one another for the whole book. Some chapters were shorter than the others, and some began with something the likes of a newspaper clipping or letter, giving a bit of background relating to the chapter and, some, the story overall, which I liked and thought was rather unique.

The majority of the art, (i.e. scenery, clothing, and double panels,) is beautiful. But a lot of it also felt amateurish, especially character's bodies and faces, there wasn't enough detailing to make proper facial expressions, most emotions were conveyed with overly exaggerated scared faces or sad eyes.

For most of the story I didn't have any particular feelings about the main characters. In retrospect, I feel like Vincent was the do-anything-for-the-girl type and Dinah would let him, however he is the one who dragged her into places she didn't want to go, and by doing that, set the plot itself in motion, so he did cause a bit of his own anguish. By the Final chapters though, Dinah was pulling more of her own weight. Seeing that things were more equal, it made me want to continue reading to see how the characters and story develop. …

Ah, The age old tale of... nope, wrong story.

A normal girl with the special ability to see spirits and interact with the magical realm, Misao Harada, always had to deal with annoying spirits, tripping and tugging at her, until she turned sixteen. On her birthday, she now has to deal with demons of every clan coming after her to make her either their; bride, so their clan will prosper, drink her blood to be guaranteed a long life, or eat her flesh for eternal youth. Only one demon seems to be on her side, the Tengu clan leader who was once Misao's childhood best friend, Kyo. Will Kyo be able to convince Misao of his love to become his bride, or is all of the heroics an act?

I read this series a long time ago, and now that I'm older, I see things a bit differently, but I'm still enjoying this series quite a bit. There is a bit of an age gap since Misao is sixteen and Kyo's age isn't definite, in fun fact a section of the book the artist says that she imagines him to be around twenty, but he looks to be at about eighteen to twenty. There are a few common shojo tropes in this, like (perceived) destined lovers and such.

One thing I really like is how strong Misao is. She may get knocked down and licked when she is in a fight was a demon, but the way she corrals Kyo and speaks her mind feels refreshing for a shojo Manga.

The art is a nice combination of hard and soft lines, but always refined. It's very pretty to look at.

I am looking forward to reading the rest of the series and see how things progress between the main Duo. And see more Taro, Kyo's little attendant, he's so cute.

Off to Tengu village!

With the demon prophecy even more of a mystery than in the beginning, Misao and Kyo ring in the New Year and decide to visit Kyo's home to visit his grandfather, who is putting pressure on the two to marry and consummate their relationship. Will Misao, the bride of prophecy, get answers at Tengu no Sato? Or will she just wind up in deeper trouble?

I am absolutely loving this series! Even when Misao is crying or may seem weak, the amount of strength she shows in dangerous and heart-wrenching situations is beautiful. Even though it's not a lot, its fun seeing Kyo's home and hearing from the people who knew him when he was younger and separated from Misao.

It's great seeing character introductions, little tidbits from the author, and art from fan requests scattered throughout the volumes plus the cover pages for each chapter is black & white, but you can tell at one point they were colored, I'd love to see those in color.

I just finished volume 5 of 18 of writing this, and I can't wait to get to the higher volumes.

The prodigal father returns.

With the sudden re-emergence of Kyo's father and attacks using human puppets still ongoing, chateau Tengu is one busy place. What clan is behind the attacks? What information does Kyo's father hold? Not only about the current situation, but about the mysterious circumstances surrounding his wife's death, and why he was blamed for it. And will an old enemy rear his head...

With the age gap of Kyo and Misao, along with Kyo's teasing meanness, I can understand how this might not be everyone's cup of tea. But I feel like everything is handled as delicately as possible and it's volumes like this that keep the urge to keep reading alive. There's twist and turns, and exciting antics on every page!

It was great getting to learn more about Kyo's family history, seeing Misao growth of emotional strength and maturity, and witnessing a softer side of Kyo, (which is flipping adorable!) While there was less action in this volume, the political element between clans and within the Tengu clan itself was interesting to say the least.

The art was also stunning! I can't wait to see where the story goes and watch the character's lives unfold. Only 8 more volumes to go.

Doppelgangers all around!

Four strangers make a suicide pact online, when they meet up in person to commit the deed, their lives get turned upside down by their own mirror images. A shadow, a robot, and the person staring back at you in the mirror are all ways to a wondrous land of light - and death. Will these four strangers complete their pact by their own hands or will they turn their lives around but die in the process... Or who knows, they may all live to tell the tale of the black paradox.

The entire vibe of this manga felt like a horror movie, and I don't mean just because of the gore, the scares, and the suspense. There's a certain presence in older horror movies, especially from the 90s, that just gives you the creeps and all the feels, that same je ne sais quoi was in Black Paradox. At first, I had no idea what was going on and was a bit confused because some of the elements didn't quite fit in the beginning, but by the end, it made complete utterly terrifying sense.

There were a lot of twists and turns, the plot was solid, and while the characters at times were a bit obnoxious, they were definitely engaging. It almost felt like the characters got what they deserved by the end, which I felt was pretty cool as they started off wanting to end their lives. But that's not to say that the ending was... necessarily good for the characters, but it felt satisfying.

I can't say much more without spoilers, so I'll just stop here by saying this is probably one of the best stories I read by Junji Ito, and it is absolutely perfection for the spooky season!

A vampire in a cat hoodie and a young surly priest...

Mary, a frail priest, constantly hunted by vampires due to his ancestors' special power-giving blood, is protected by the very thing that tries to kill him, Bloody Mary, yet another vampire. But Mary is a bit different than your average vampire, namely that he has little memory of his past, and that he begs Maria to kill him. The deal is simple; Mary becomes Maria's bodyguard in exchange for Maria learning how to harness his ancestral power to kill vampires and then kill Mary. Sounds fair, doesn't it?

First off, Mary is absolutely freaking adorable. His little cat ear hoodie, dark eyebags, and child-like demeanor make me want to hug and protect him and take him away from that prick Maria. While I understand that Maria has a lot going on, what with vampires constantly trying to kill him, unexplained secrets, and such, he basically blackmails Mary into being his bodyguard and treats him so badly.

Maria's rude behavior aside, the story is very interesting. A lot of hints are given out to through this volume, and I really have no idea where they could possibly go. But what I'm most curious about is Mary's past. Why is Mary's so different from other vampires? His red hair, his amnesia, the fact he had the ability to walk in sunlight.

Hopefully, Maria warms up to Mary, which it looks like he will from little bits here and there. I am so here for the wild and bloody ride these two are about to embark on!

There's no shame in my game.

Ryo is the average boy, he has a crush on a girl in his class, has decent grades, and likes basketball, art (aka graffiti,) and his biggest passion, men's clothing. Problem is, his body is that of a girl and that's how people see him, as something, (someone,) he's not. Will the new delinquent looking transfer student, but kind-hearted Jin, help Ryo come to terms with being himself, free him from being the dreaded outcast, and help him run a fashion empire?

Boys Run the Riot exceeded my expectations! I knew I'd like this, but there's so much love that went into this book it morphed into having a life of its own. The emotions in this volume really hit home, not in the same way as Ryo, but you could feel his anger, excitement, sadness, loneliness, etc. jump off the page. Ryu is a great character and there was so much growth in this one volume that I'm so excited to see his progress through the rest of the 3 volumes in the series, but my favorite character is Jin. He is so supportive and stubborn; he is a friend that anyone would be lucky to have.

The art is gorgeous! The characters look realistic, even though they do have the signature big manga eyes, they feel more natural than most.  One thing though, some of the boy's noses or mouths had lines which made them look more natural, however also made them look incredibly older for their age. Even Ryo's artistic talent is great, I can't wait to see what work he does in the further volumes.

This is a fantastic slice of life, true LGBTQ manga that should be on everyone's shelves.

Best LGBTQ+ manga out there!

This was the perfect ending to this short four-volume series! I don't want to give anything away, but I will say that even in the face of adversity, these three kids and their friends really stepped up for one another, and would stop at nothing to help each other, no matter who - or what - they are. This whole series, the story is focused on design and fashion, but the heart and soul of this series is about understanding yourself and finding others who will encourage yet give you the room to explore different aspects of yourself without judgment.

I love how the art isn't typical shonen or shojo style with the overly large, odd pupil eyes and cartoonish physicality of the characters. Everything was well proportioned and realistic, which really drew me in and made the whole story feel even more genuine. You will definitely feel all the feelings with this one: anger, joy, sadness, giddiness, everything right along with these characters and for these characters.

I do wish the story had focused a little bit more on Jin throughout the series, along with some of the other side characters, so they would've felt a bit more fleshed out. But I do understand the focus being on Ryo and Tsubasa; a lot of the discussion of the series is about gender and how it is portrayed, and the feelings of it not matching your physical body. Also, the poignant short story titled "Light" at the end of this volume That what inspired Boys Run the Riot was the cherry on top. It had the same heart, adversities, intolerance, and acceptance that the whole series had, just scaled down for a one-shot.

Overall, a thoughtful and thought-provoking series, with a main cast that will grab your heart, never let go, and make you want to burn the world down to rebuild it. I will forever recommend this series to anyone who will let me rant about its awesomeness.

Live in the night until the day gets better.
4 1/2* stars.

So much love and attention went into not only the art and relationships, *wink wink*, but the world-building was off the charts! I really did not expect that, not from a spicy BL manga, but this series delivered.

Even the (seemingly) ridiculous concept worked so well in the setting; the whole thing was pretty down-to-earth. We even have Matthew to thank for establishing that, to the outside world of the archipelago, this tournament is completely weird! His point of view made things feel even more grounded and oddly realistic. There was no use of H logic, like, "Well, this is good to go right off the bat, let's stick it in!" and took the time and care to explain that you can't just dive in, so to speak, that some preparation is needed, especially if one is not used to— *ahem*.

Don't get me wrong, that was plenty of goofy moments and hilarity; this manga kept me in stitches, giggling, laughing, rolling off my seat guffawing. Not to mention the majority of the characters were well fleshed out in this volume, and the ones that were only touched on - no pun intended - I had hoped were more even developed in the second volume. And did I mention the art? It was stunning! Between the island, the men, their armor, everything was very detailed and beautifully drawn!

Sweet heat with an Island twist.

Summary:
The perfect conclusion to an absolutely absurd, yet wonderfully done yoai/spicy BL!! The art was just as detailed as volume 1, and I loved seeing the characters' lives after the well-fought tournament and learning more about them. I will recommend this to anyone who would be interested; this series must have more love!

Full review:
Oh my gosh. I could absolutely lose the battle of life from the cuteness and spice in the series, but particularly in this volume! The tournament may have been over, but the islands' - and characters' - lore kept a-coming! As did the men. The first volume could've been a one-shot; yeah, I was curious about some of the characters and how they ended up, but after finishing volume two, I now realize how much I neeeeeded the closure from the couples from the tournament. Those that participated and the king, his advisor, and even the nondescript referee of the tournament gets his chance at lov—

Uh, well... he got his just desserts, but I liked the fact that every character got a proper resolution. The characters didn't just have endings, though. Some of the characters from volume one that didn't get much screen time but still had little hints of things happening in the background, were fleshed out more, giving full life to the men of the island. And Britain!

Yes, that is right, we get to see how Matthew and Hart(o?) met! And how they cohabitate now, ooh la la, hehe. In all seriousness, though, the backstory felt a little jarring, but it was so nice to see how their relationship grew from startled flatmates to full lovers. It was also lovely to see Matthew being a protective friend/crush in a healthy way; no touch him and die energy, but the feels were perfect.

My only gripe is that most of the names were spelled differently from the first volume to the second, which made it a little hard for me to identify who the characters were talking about if they were not in the scene. …

"This is Halloween, this is halloween~"

Everyday is Halloween in Halloween Town, but Jack Skellington, the pumpkin king, ruler of Halloween Town, and master of all things ooky and spooky, is tired of the same humdrum kookiness. When he accidentally comes upon Christmas Town, he decides that's his chance to liven things up by creating a new holiday, Scary Christmas! But the sweet patchwork doll Sally believes that the holidays do not mesh like that and tries to dissuade Jack, but the pumpkin king cannot be stopped, until things go awry... Can Jack and Sally set things right before Christmas is ruined?

As a fan of the movie, I feel like little bits and pieces were missing, but I can't even place what they are, so it did not impact the story at all. Speaking of the story, flipping through the pages and seeing the familiar faces gave me such a sense of nostalgia! Seeing these beloved characters in black & white in my favorite format (manga) was such a treat!

The art was gorgeous, and the lines were soft, giving the book a light and airy feeling so it didn't feel too dark even with all of the creepy fun characters and details. And the iconic scene with Sally and Jack on the curly hill was beautiful, along with an almost glittery Zero.

As a fan of the movie or not, this was an amazingly fun read for any age. Also by Tokyopop, centered around the bestest ghost dog in Halloween Town, Zero!

The feels are confusing from this one.

The art is good, the facial expressions are really on point, and the story is... Well, I feel conflicted.

The first two chapters was a bit of a rough start for me, I felt that this underclassman, later to be found out as Nagatoro, is a really mean and cruel little girl, yet, there was something that sucked you in.  Maybe it was the little bit of kindness she showed after bullying Senpai into tears, or maybe it was the thought I had in my head that she was a shy girl who liked the manga Senpai drew but was too shy to admit it, or it was the fact that she worried if she went too far after she left their first meeting. I really don't know.

By chapter 3 it got a little better as we learned a bit more about Senpai, and how he sees Nagatoro's teasing as teasing and not cruel bullying like he's sadly used to, and by chapter 5 we learned a bit about Nagatoro also, getting to know the characters made it a bit more amusing to watch Nagatoro, tease? torture? toy, with Senpai.

It is a fun read once you get into it, and when the mood strikes, I do believe I'll find myself picking up more volumes of Don't Toy With Me, Miss Nagatoro!

If nothing else just to see where the story goes and to see if they can turn this odd relationship that they have into an actual friendship.

Or maybe even a full-blown relationship, who knows.

What are funeral shoes and why a lizard head?

Review summary:
The story is dark with spots of deadpan humor and gruesomely delicious art. There is a lot going on on both the protag- and antagonist sides, and I'm here for it all. I cannot wait to get my hands on more volumes to see what transpires.

Full review:
I had sampled this on the Viz Media site and fell in love with the main character's, Caiman's, design and his quest to find the sorcerer who cast the spell that turned his head into a lizard's. Also, why is there a talking head in the lizard's throat?! That simple premise sucked me right into the world. But throughout the whole volume, I found myself more drawn to the sorcerers' part of the story rather than Caiman and his friend, Nikaido.

The sorcerers' magic system and powers, their social norms and masks, and how they came to be in their own world. Their side of the story stirred up a lot of questions I really want answered, so much so that I felt like Caiman's story was secondary to En - the head sorcerer - and his people, despite Nikaido and Caiman's actions leading En to go after the duo.

The art was well detailed and gritty, just like the Hole; the characters' city, and the bloodshed and butchery were fabulously gruesome. I'm a bit of a horror junkie, and I loved the fantastical carnage. Seeing the Hole was fun, and I do have some questions surrounding it, but it felt kind of repetitive as the Duo just found sorcerers, seeing if the head in Caiman's throat recognized them, and then unalived them. I really hope they get a little more depth in future volumes, but I did enjoy the sometimes random bits of deadpan humor from them.

Subura is best girl.

I love my brothers but I would also appreciate a sister like her... Or I might be that sister, hmm.

I can relate to Hinako, trying to fit in by doing what people think one should do to seem "normal."  I've always been told what is normal and that everyone has their own normal,  which through the story there is steady character development, especially highlighting Hinako's thought processes and self discoveries.

I really like Asahi's confidence, how she does her own thing, and her work ethic. Their relationship starts and grows organically at a steady albeit slightly slow pace with plenty of sweet moments that made me want to cheer on the friends/ couple.

I recommend this down-to-earth yuri for a slow burn romance that's worth sticking around to see the end.
3.5* stars. Feels pretty basic for a high school romance. But there is some mystery to it and the humor is good, so I rounded my rating up.

Sunday morning manga

3 1/2* stars

I tried reading Fairy Tail about a decade ago, who doesn't love wizards right? But I just couldn't get into it. I picked it up again a couple years back, found a liking for it but didn't stick with it. Now, I believe the third time is the charm! I've started watching the anime and, read the first volume. Again.

There's enough to keep my attention to read through it but, to me, Fairy Tail is one of those books/mangas that you want to read for a laugh on Sunday morning, not a series you would want to read every day of the week.

There is a touch of fanservice, but I don't believe it is inappropriate for any age.

The art matches the vibe of the story very well, there are even Godfather-esque angles delivering well-timed dramatics to some of the scenes giving the story a little more depth, but not too much as to scare off any kiddos just wanting some light hearted wizarding fun.

There is not much I can say other than, I do intend to keep reading, but only when the urge strikes.

I've never read a Simon Snow book but Fangirl has made me want to.

I have not read the novel [b:Fangirl|16068905|Fangirl|Rainbow Rowell|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1355886270l/16068905._SX50_.jpg|21861351], however I really want to after reading this manga adaptation. All of the characters were so relatable one way or another, and minus the crippling social anxiety (in the beginning) I basically am Cath. Or aspiring to be her with her passion for words and awesome writing skills, also henceforth major reader following. While it could be considered a codependent trait on Cath's part, I believe the worriment and watching out for her family more comes from a place of love then personal need.

The art is beautiful block lines situated in a 1 to 5 panel skits, the cover is red fabric with black and embossing good matches the story perfectly.

Spontaneous human combustion. Yeowch...

4.5* stars, rounded up for full omnibus volume. 4* stars for single volume one.
His first step to achieving his dream of becoming a hero, like he promised his mother he would, Shinra joined the Special Fire Cathedral 8. This team is tasked with discovering the source of the deadly phenomenon plaguing the city of Tokyo: spontaneous human combustion! He's known as Third Gen, meaning he is blessed with the ability to ignite fire from his feet and travel faster than a racing car. But Shinra's haunting past follows him, along with the cruel moniker, Devil's Footprints. Will he become the hero he dreams of, or will the fires of his past prove he is a devil?

This is a really fun start. Shinra has a lot of things to work through relating to his past, but he's a very likable character and someone that's easy to root for. Some of the characters are reminiscent of [b:Soul Eater, Vol. 1|6406018|Soul Eater, Vol. 1|Atsushi Ohkubo|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1443900841l/6406018._SY75_.jpg|6594903] characters, but their designs and personalities are totally different. I like to see how similar yet progressed the art is between different series written/drawn by the same person. I just think it's fun to notice the differences.

The world is interesting, and I am looking forward to getting to know all the characters, but I can't say it is super different from other shonen series; however, it does stick out in its own right with its premise. I also like how the majority of the art is bold and has thick lines, yet it has stellar detailing, even for innocuous things in the background. And the fire looks so good!

This review is only for the single volume one, even though I'm currently reading the omnibus set. I'm still going to review volumes one, five, ten, etc., and also put them on the corresponding omnibus volumes that house those single volumes. …

Another fire volume!

4.5 stars for the single and omnibus volume.
Learning from the Joker that his younger brother Shō is not only alive but running a group within the Evangelist/whitehood organization, Shinra relies on Company 8, his new family, to help find him as their investigation into the organization deepens. After what happened in Company 1, the entire Fire Force decides to set their sights on the Evangelist to stop them from creating more infernals. Company 8 finds a clue that leads them to Asakusa, Company 7's jurisdiction. But after a manufactured mistaken identity mishap, Captain Obi must duke it out with the captain of Company 7 - the strongest in the force - Benjimaru, before he'll listen to reason.

The story has progressed well so far! The art is fantastic, and the characters are hilarious and sometimes dim-witted, but they have big hearts and tend to think things through before they act, which is a nice change of pace when reading a lot of shonen series. Speaking of thinking, the revelation that Shinra's little brother, Shō, is not only part of the White Hood organization but is a leader in it!? That came out of nowhere. I mean, I figured he had to be alive just out of reader hope and, come on, he had to be. Shinra would be heartbroken otherwise.

It's been really fun getting to know all the interesting characters in the Fire Force world. One thing, though, within the fifth volume, some of the panels seemed to be jumping a little bit. Nothing too drastic, but it tended to pull me out of the story a bit. I checked back to see if I missed something, but I hadn't. Hopefully, that will smooth out and not become a recurring pattern.

Overall, a great action series with heart and a lot of thought put into it that I am excited to continue reading!

Let the Shō-w down begin!

4.5* stars.
Review summary:
The feels and action are strong with this volume. I love the quirkiness of the characters and seeing Shinra's growth as a fire soldier, but also as a young man. To volume 11, let's go!

Full review:
Things are really heating up in Fire Force, I love how almost everything in this volume was Shinra and his little brother Shō, basically being brothers, despite Shō's lack of memory and brattiness - Shinra's phrasing. It's also really cool that, apparently, subways are a thing of the past in the Fire Force world, the underground tunnels now considered a taboo and scary place. Being underground, it's where "the light of Amaterasu cannot reach," essentially being the boogie man for ill-behaved kids. It's still unnerving even for adults too, and the entrances are off limits without written consent with the government.

I love how throughout the whole series even in the serious parts there's a bit (or a lot) of jokes and lighthearted scenes. Though lately, some of the more serious notes have been a little jarring. Like how the team 8's new scientist, Licht, explained to Shinra how heat could make time slow or even stop in the middle of a major fight - that Shinra was in - or the rather corny medical dramatics. Don't get me wrong, I'm rather intrigued how an entire fire company based out of a hospital as a medical unit along with firefighting works in this world, but the team's introduction still felt corner than the normal silliness of the series.

That said, I am glad I have the omnibuses and can keep reading, because I need to learn more about the Evangelist and what their plan is for Shinra and the other Adolla Burst or fourth gen people. And of course see how Shinra is able to get his brother back, because let's be real, he has to convince Shō to come to his side, right!?... Right?

3.5* stars.
Neat premise, entertaining action, fun characters, just nothing overly spectacular.

La de da, a stroll through the woods for 50 years.

That is the vibe of the series, not that it drags on forever but how peaceful the time flows.  This book is so relaxing yet makes me want to adventure at the same, I don't know what magic it holds but if following volumes are just as good it may wind up in my top 5 manga.

Through most of it there doesn't seem to be much of a plot line but as things progress little tid-bits here and there tend to make sense, hinting that while something may not seem important at the moment it will be integral to something else later down the road.

The art matches this sweet story well, and artistically speaking the character's appearance ages with them. It's not only hairstyles that change, you can see their facial features age through the years, particularly with Fern. I feel this is important to note because I find with most series as a character gets older the only change you see is their hair or clothes, not a physical change so I think it's a very nice attention to detail.

I read this a matter of two days about a week ago and I already want to re-read it, to me it's one of those stories that stick with you.

Frieren is a series I am in love with!

In this volume we see Frieren and Fern split into separate teams to capture a iron bird called a Stille, pitted against more mages, to pass the exam on the road to become a first class mage.

It was really fun seeing Frieren's magical know-how and ingenuity in catching the Stille. I also really like all the characters that were introduced, they're gonna be fun to learn more about in the coming volumes. The characters have their own quarks, but are lovable folks that you and I would like to hang out with.

Over the past 5 volumes we have gotten to know Frieren and her party members pretty well too. And man, I really wish fern (Frieren's mage apprentice,) and Stark (the party's warrior, (who, based off his looks, reminds me of Shoto Todoroki from [b:My Hero Academia, Vol. 1|25074597|My Hero Academia, Vol. 1 (My Hero Academia, #1)|Kohei Horikoshi|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1426466596l/25074597._SX50_.jpg|43165801],)) would just talk openly and admit that they like each other.

The volumes I've read have come from my library, but this is one series I want to read over and over again, so I'm definitely going get my own copies, and I can't wait for volume 6!

A story of environmental struggles, personified!

4.5* stars.
Summary:
With the intrigue, mystery, and action, this volume could hook anyone! There's cool art, a unique magic system, and an environmentally conscious message, all of which were a joy to read. I would recommend this to absolutely anyone who liked anything mentioned above.

Full review:
This is most assuredly a love letter to everyone about taking better care of the environment and of the things in our lives. The message of the story was blatant but well delivered; it was reminiscent of [b:Cells at Work!, Vol. 1|29844802|Cells at Work!, Vol. 1|Akane Shimizu|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1474765845l/29844802._SX50_.jpg|50204347], about how taking care of one section of your body helps take care of it all. How we care for the objects in our lives can tell a story about how we take care of our fellow humans (and other creatures). Okay, yes, I may be overthinking a bit, heck, I probably am, but that was the moral I got from reading Gachiakuta, and I really liked it.

Now, for the actual story. I liked how the first chapter was essentially an epilogue. It was a nice setup for the world, and while it was a little jarring going from that to the second chapter in a completely different setting, it was still a good setup and made me prepared for what happened a bit more in the second world, a.k.a. The Pit. I'm really curious how the mystery that started in the first setting - the Sphere - is going to play out now that Rudo got "dropped" into The Pit.

The action was on point and at many times unexpected, in the best of ways! Each page left me on my toes, wanting more, and more, and more. The art was really cool and oftentimes gave a bit of a horror vibe with the intense facial close-ups. I love horror, so that was awesome. But overall, the art was simultaneously perfect for action, but also silly, and a bit uncanny. …

Ghosts, monsters, and ghouls, with a side of mystery, oh my!

Review summary:
There's nothing particularly special so far in the first of this three-volume series, but I do feel like there is promise here. Fun antics with a bunch of ghost-hunting kids and an exorcist, who tries to find his missing, spirited away sister. How can you not at least try Ghost Diary?

Full review:
Ghost Diary was a really fun read, and there's nothing wrong with it, though I can't really think of anything in particular that stood out as special. I love ghost detectives, so the idea of Kyouichi's friends in the Occult Club investigating paranormal mysteries, with the help - and at the peril of - his exorcist powers, pulled me in. One thing I was not a fan of was that the story plays into the little brother/big sister crush trope. It was handled well enough, and there was nothing overt except for repeating jokes and mentions of it by Kyouichi's friends, especially Miyumi, who has a crush on him, but it just started feeling redundant after a while.

Despite the overreaching arc of trying to find Hanaichi, Kyouichi's sister, there was a "ghost-a-week" quality to the story, which I enjoyed. The designs of the entities the kids dealt with weren't very original in my opinion. Except for one macaron ghost, he was pretty neat. I also felt like there was a bit of unnecessary fan service, which didn't detract from the story, nor was it "heavy", so to speak, but I felt like it could have done without it.

The dialogue also felt a bit choppy in places. However, that could have been issues with the translation, not the actual story. The mystery of the lost sister is intriguing: I think I have an idea of where it's going, but this three-volume series is going to be fun, I can already tell.

Not perfect, but a solid, short series.

Review summary:
For only 3 volumes, this was worth my time for something quick and fun. I feel like there were some things that could have been done better, and the sister/brother crush trope gave me the ick at times, but that stuff could be overlooked for the fun and cool folklore of the monsters, Gods, and ghosts of the series.

Full review:
This was... wow. First off, I don't know why it happened, but, WHY WOULD SAEKI DO THAT!? I can't say what happened because it would be a pretty decent spoiler, but I don't feel like the resolving emotions between the characters were earned. It felt too quick. I'm also genuinely confused as to why that had to have happened. I don't feel like it furthered the story; it at most made Saeki less likable, which didn't make sense as he was still a "good guy" by the end. Speaking of the end, I felt like the main story ended in the middle of this volume. I thought everything was pretty well summed up, until the last three pages of chapter twelve.

Through the next and final chapters, I felt like it was just an extension, like a side quest. There were some stray loose ends that were tied up, and some pretty neat lore/haunts, so I'm okay with it. Especially since it allowed us to have the true end to Ghost Diary, and that ending I felt was well deserved. Through all of it, the main plot was a little predictable, and some of the side mysteries were too, but there were enough twists and turns to keep me guessing, and definitely enough action to keep me entertained.

All the characters were pretty likable, including Saeki until the thing in this volume, and I like how the main characters switched a little bit by the end of the series. I felt bad for two of the side characters, but one of the characters - again, I don't want to give spoilers - deserved a possibly slightly better ending, but considering the circumstances of everything, they got the best ending they could have. "I promise I'll die with you."

What if one day you woke up and could turn into a monster mascot suit? That is what Shuichi Kagaya is dealing with. He's a smart, but people-pleasing kid that should be thinking about his future. However instead, due to a chance meeting with a classmate, Claire Aoki, Shuichi is pulled into a dangerous coin-collecting "game" started by an unknown boy. But Claire and Shuichi's quest began with a bloody scene caused by Claire's sister... Will the Duo survive long enough to find out about Shuichi's new transformation, what the coins are for, and what Claire's sister had to do with this?

Overall, this is a very intriguing story and there's a lot of twist and turns and unanswered questions. But there's one thing I don't get; the point of the highly sexually suggestive and more-than-necessary panty shots/fan service parts. Other than shock value or to appear more edgy, there really is no need for the explicit content in my opinion, it is not necessary and the story would be just as good without it. That is my reasoning for only giving this volume three and a half stars.

Now the story itself, like I said, is very interesting, I really want to know what is up with Claire's sister, especially after the cliffhanger flashback. And why a dog mascot with a gun? Also, what's so special about these coins? A bit is told about them within this volume, but not enough to really understand their true meaning.

The art is also pretty nice, the characters I feel have a touch of Western influence in their designs, while still sticking with general manga style of course, but the touch of Western really helps with making the monsterish designs look a bit more realistic and not so out of the ordinary for the world, even though it technically is.

With all these questions I definitely want to read on and hope that the sexual stuff wanes so I can get answers! …

Mascot or not, killing is inevitable.

Joining forces with new allies, Shuichi and Claire are on the hunt for a spaceship and one hundred coins in the mountains, but they are not alone out there. The foes they've fought thus far don't hold a candle to the gangs of "aliens" higher in the mountains, including a group with Claire's sister. Not only must they struggle to keep their lives, they must also strive for coins or the whole world could be in danger.

This volume was action packed, so much happened not only with our heroine's side, but with the backstage characters too. Claire has been a bit psychopathic all the way through the series so far, and it's a bit sad to see her drag Shuichi down to her level, but we also see Claire's remorse stronger too. Seeing the different sides really rounds out both characters well, along with a morally gray bad guy that would do anything for his men while having no qualms about killing other collectors. There have been a lot of tough decisions by the characters through this series, but it was refreshing to see someone, the bad guy, so strongly cling too his principles in contrast to Shuichi unraveling his.

The art is well done, particularly the designs of the monsters/aliens are really cool, and the action/fight scenes have been wonderfully illustrated. I also like how pretty quick after the first volume, it was corrected that the monsters are actually aliens and are addressed as such now, adding a bit of a sci-fi level to the series that weirdly makes sense even though there isn't any normal sci-fi tropes going on that I'm aware of. And thankfully, the unnecessary fan service has toned down quite a bit too, so it's easier to concentrate more on the plot and mysteries than a random sexual scene.

All in all, the series is progressing nicely, and I am definitely looking forward to catching up on the rest of the 14 volumes!

This may be the best LGBTQ+ manga out there!

What happens when two friends realize they're both lesbians? They date, obviously. While that may seem absurd on the surface, there is so much heart and love in this relationship that it works out great for reserved Miwa and outgoing Saeko.

The different struggles couples have to go through, jealousy, why do they like me, am I being a pain, when is the right time for the "next step." And it gives an extra kick with the LGBTQ+ element of, is it ok to tell this person we're dating, how will they react to me dating a girl, will we be outed, and so forth.

Everything is illustrated beautifully and it's great that the side characters get chapters from their point of view, so we not only see the main couple's struggles and successes, but we also get closer to their friends, and see how they feel in their life. Oh, and did I mention there's a music club? I had no idea that there was a music element to this book which just makes it an even more incredible read.

I love this series so much! I'd recommend this series to anyone who'll listen, but especially folks that like romance, realistic couples and storylines, slice of life genre, and a comfort read with some drama.

The premise of the landlady's "service" contract is so out there it can never happen, but it's so logical (albeit slightly illegal I believe) that it's oddly believable. At least in manga that is. While it is an odd start to a relationship, it works.

The story flowed well and the characters were realistic and complimentary to one another, and the mystery of Landlady-san's affection for Koduka is curious, it left me wanting to know more. One little irk for me though was that Koduka was a bit of a crybaby. And please know I don’t say that lightly as I myself can be emotional at the worst and best of times lol.

The art was cute and airy and didn't show anything particularly naughty in detail but I would recommend this manga for mature minded readers. But I guess the title is a hint at that already, wink.

Meet cute part 2: The original.

For such an absurd preface to a relationship the ending result is pretty balanced, Koduka falls for Ritsu (yes that is Landlady-san's name) in a organic way, coming into herself at the same time. While the reason of Landlady-san's affection for Koduka from the beginning is revealed. (That backstory, phew.)

The art is still light and airy,  giving the series a sweet and bubbly atmosphere. This is a bit spicier than the other 2 volumes but it is done in a tasteful way and does not show details of anything explicit. the most candid images would be silhouettes of breasts, and at that it's not eye catching.

I really like the side characters, they're fun, quirky, and real like the main couple. Also there is a possible Ace representation too. Which doesn't mean much to the main story, I just happen to like the character's personality and wish she had a bit more page time.

This is a very fun series and I wish it lasted longer than just 3 volumes but some things are just at their best when they're short and sweet.

It's a sheep eat wolf world out there...

There is no improper species consumption in this series, only cuteness overload. Oogami, the only wolf in a all sheep department of a bedding company, fights his natural predatory instincts everyday to keep his cool in front of Mitsuji, his strong seeming sheep department head. While Oogami has a certain puppy-dog air about him, Mitsuji is the one whom everyone in the department loves. Can a wolf and sheep really make it work in the world of bedding and linens?!

 If I have anything to say about it, yes they will. This was a really fun volume, I was not expecting the chapters to be short and episodic,  but I believe it worked very well, especially since the chapters carried over the whole story to make a plot instead of individual episodes. All of the characters are interesting folks, the side characters even got a bit of attention to make them more then props, which is nice.

The art is cute and airy, but still down to earth, and I love the character's animal characteristics. It's interesting that their animal ears don't actually work, nor aid in them hearing any better, it's just an evolutionary trait! As a monster girl/person lover, that's just flipping awesome and kinda unique for the trope.

This series is such a hoot, I can't wait to learn more about the other characters, the animal characteristics, and seeing if Oogami gets the girl. Especially with that cliff hanger, oof!

Not quite what I was expecting... It's better than!

I love monster girls/people so I'm always looking for new series to try.  This is a easy series to read, it's perfect for a rainy afternoon,  Summer read in the park or beach, or better yet, all snuggled up in bed as a comfort read. Also the 4 panel skits at the end of each chapter is a nice bonus.

The characters are all so genuine in their personalities and true to their selves, even those who are not exactly comfortable being a Demi, (no one says Demi-humens, it's not cute enough. That comes straight from the vamps mouth so you know it's gotta be true lol.)

On the surface it could be misconstrued as a harem manga but the usual tropes and shenanigans aren't there. Takahashi-sensei is a mature guy who has almost farther-like feelings towards the students in his care, to the point of feeling a need to protect and comfort them.

Even the succubus math teacher, he takes care to not let her see the effect her powers (of arousal with just a touch) have on him because she doesn't want to unintentionally harm others, she is self conscious about it and goes to great pains to play down her powers.

The kids are kids and the adults are mature which is a nice thing to see in a monster girl series. It reminds me of My Life As a Centaur; kids going through their teenage years and navigating the troubles and tribulations of it.

I would recommend Interviews with Monster Girls to someone looking for a unusual coming of age story, a slice of life with a twist (especially of the supernatural or fantastical kind), or anyone who enjoy manga.

Not for the faint of heart... in multiple ways

3.5* stars.
What if Hell was like our everyday lives, except for, you know, demons and torture? That's what Rintaro, a mid-20s everyday man, finds out after he accidentally bonks his head drunk one night and finds himself met with the beautiful, petite demon, Koyori, in Hell. She becomes Rintaro's guide to their little circle of Hell, explaining how he can make an income to live a better life here, and of course, how his daily torture sessions will work for the remainder of his multi-decade sentence! Can Rintaro figure out why he was sent to Hell when he had led such an unassuming life? And why won't Koyori help him learn of his sinful indiscretions? The answers to those and many other questions lie solely within this complete omnibus of the three-volume series.

There are a lot of things going on in this book. Like, a lot. Sinners being tortured - skinned alive, - demons in ridiculous but adorable and sexy outfits, and the fictional Amazon company of Hell. This story is like the town of Hell Live in Hell is set in, a melting pot of a little bit of everything. And while this is not for the faint of heart as there is some nudity, crude jokes, talk of torture, and all manners of death of all ages of people, and sex, it all strangely works!

The story is compelling, especially the world-building of the system regarding the demons and their assigned sinners. When a sinner arrives, they are automatically assigned to a demon and their torture for redemption begins. The demon can tell how much torture the sinner has left due to a handy smartphone app: if a sinner gets their demon's emblem tattooed onto themselves, the demon can track their movements wherever the sinner is! Not to mention how the sinners can make a living and live in the equivalent of high-rises while still being tortured daily. It's fascinating! …

The beautiful boy in black.

As I read the first story, Lovesickness, I was thinking that, "Wow, this is my new favorite story!" Then I read The Strange Hikizuri Siblings, that had since became my favorite. And I read The Rib Woman and... well the Hikizuri Siblings is the most intriguing storyline to me, but all of them are incredibly beautiful and haunting, and my new favorite in some way.

Although the last story is just odd lol.

The art is stunning, so eerie it stays with you. While uneasiness is in the after thoughts, the beauty of the horrors stands out to me. Not just the Beautiful Boy but all scenes, the ghosts, carnage, the everyday people and things.

I'm a fan of Edger Allen Poe, while most see darkness and sadness, I see the light of his works, that’s what stands out to me. Poe and Ito share that light in the dark, beauty in the horror. That delicate balance is what draws me to what some consider disturbing written/art works.

One day Junji Ito manga will grace my shelves in all its hardbacked glory, but until then I'm raiding my local library for more ghoulish delight.

The pacing is perfect. A slow boil, but with visible progress that lets you know things are happening. Most of the chapters are small, only about 4 to 5 pages long, except for half chapters that were a bit longer, (about 15 or so pages if I remember right,) and I feel if the chapters were longer the series could lose its charm. The chemistry between our two love birds was almost palpable, leaping off the screen.

The cute shyness of both parties and slight oblivion on Fuyutsuki's part about Himuro and her own feelings, and when Fuyutsuki gave Himuro a sand drum so he could get used to the sound of the ocean, so he wouldn't create a blizzard from excitement of seeing the ocean was the most... And I'm not gonna mention the (I'm running out of words meaning cute lol) sweet little snowmen that Himuro makes when his emotions flare. Oi, I think I'm in a diabetic coma from the sweetness. (In a good way!)

Spooky, slice of life comedy.

Review summary:
You'll be dropped into the thick of it just like Miko, the main character. As long as you're not afraid of things that go bump in the night, the combination of cuteness and horrid specters, the slice of life situations, and deadpan humor will keep you craving the next chapter.

Full review:
The beginning was a little jarring. It started in the middle of things, so I felt confused until about the third chapter. Nothing new was explained; I just got used to the creepy spirits abound in Miko's world, much like she was. While most spirits were grotesque and highly disturbing, there were also some very cute and sweet moments with lighter spirits, giving a nice balance.

This was most definitely a comedy with its deadpan humor and awkward situations, particularly with Miko's friend Hana. Which leads me to something that seemed a little odd. The first chapter, I felt, was trying a little too hard to have fan service. There was nothing inappropriate, just oddly angled panels and poses in the first chapter, then some locker room changing in the second. The changing felt more natural than the poses and such from the first chapter, so I wouldn't have thought about it normally. But the rest I have to say was relatively wholesome, given the monstrous ghosties hanging around every corner.

The spooks were really good! As a horror fan, I was pleased to see unique ghosts everywhere; not one misshapen haunt was reused. I really hope they will continue to be as unique in the future volumes. I really enjoyed the humor - Mieruko-Chan feels more comedy than horror to me - and the everyday situations that Miko had to face while dealing with her newfound ability, which thankfully for her wasn't all bad. Sometimes, even the seemingly worst kind of curse has a silver lining.

At first, I was captured by the cuteness and humor, but didn't find much particularly special about the series, but about halfway through I really saw the beauty in it. With how caring Miss Kobayashi was to her dragon roommates and Tohru's slightly delusional side but welling meaning attitude. Plus, the more that was revealed, like Kanna and Tohru's other dragon friends Lucoa and Fafnir, by the end I was craving to know more about the four dragon characters and the dragon world they come from.

There are quite a few volumes of the main story, Miss Kobayashi's Dragon Maid, and spin-off series, all of which I plan on collecting in due time.

Umekichi is best boy.

Muhyo and Roji are connected on a soul level.
4.5* stars.

I love this series and will recommend it to anyone. Particularly those who love comedy with a bit of drama and anyone with a hint of supernatural love.

Fungi girls, political intrigue, and action, all in a love story.

Two mushroom girls, Arriala the herder and Erriela the scribe, get married. What starts out as a marriage to tie tribes together in times of dwindling supplies turns into true love, but when a member of the Royal family of this all-woman planet is also in love with Erriela, she kidnaps her to become her wife! Arriala will use all of her skills and stop at nothing to get her loved one back in this single volume story.

This is a monster girl lover nerds dream! While the actual panels may not be too text heavy, between chapters there is "Shroom~pedia" that explains the different ways of the world and different techniques of how these girls/women live, along with the other fungi that inhabits the world. In the middle of the volume there is also a bonus Shroom~pedia special that describes the organisms and ecosystems of the world, the hierarchy of the planet and countries, currency, and how crimes are dealt with.

The art is absolutely stunning! The amount of detail in everything is amazing, right down to the different characters, who may look very similar to one another, but in this artist hands they are easily identifiable as long as you pay attention to details.

This may not be everyone's cup of tea, but I loved the worldbuilding and sweet wholesomeness of this book. I really wish they'd make a second story set in this world.

Wholesome within the fan service.

4.5* stars.
Marin is a beauty and the most popular girl in school; Gojo is introverted and worries about getting close to people. On the surface they seem like complete opposites, but passions are a strong driving force that bring people together. Gojo comes from a long line of traditional Japanese doll artisans, and he one day hopes to take over his family's business, but right now, his skill is next to none when making clothes. Marin may be a gyaru that looks like a fashion model, but fashion is the furthest thing from her mind as her heart lies with (erotic) games and cosplay. After a fortuitous meeting, the two realize their passions intersect and decide to team up, hoping to win a cosplay contest. It's questionable though, whether Gojo can survive all of the heart pounding seemingly "innocent" moments Marin throws at him.

Going in, I expected a lot of fan service and questionable panels, and My Dress Up Darling did not disappoint. While the lewd panels themselves were lewd, the intentions behind them and the story surrounding it were all quite innocent, for the most part, which was a nice counterbalance as a whole, but especially to the two chapters full of bikini shots.

It was fun seeing Marin and Gojo express their love for their hobbies. The excitement and passion they feel with them leapt off the pages and got me excited too. The art is soft yet defined extremely well, the expressions of the characters and their bodies were particularly detailed, helping the characters really come alive.

I was already invested, but that cliff hanger made me need more! This is definitely a series for mature minded individuals, not kids. If you can look past the scandalous moments, this is really a sweet story that I would recommend to anyone willing to give it the shot it deserves.

Devoured in a not-so-lonesome night.

Like others, she touched on things that I deal with on a daily basis, lack of motivation, eagerness to win parents approval, to be liked, the glittering strength of coming out of depression then bottoming out again, ect.. It was refreshing, and a bit inspiring, to read something so open and honest in the best book format in the world.

I can appreciate the strength it took in detailing intimate parts of her life for the sake of getting published and living out her dream as a mangaka. The art is simple with a pink and white aesthetic adding to uniqueness of a manga memoir, perfection for the material and vibe of the story.

I read this book online, in one night, and I plan to purchase a physical copy and the sequels.

Nothing groundbreaking, but adorable nonetheless!

Review summary:
The review title says it all. Both volumes of My Secret Affection are a sweet and fluffy school romance with a hearty dose of personal growth and self-acceptance in the face of a world that would call you wrong. If you want a short, easy read, I definitely recommend this two-volume series.

Full review:
It's a really neat concept of meteors making everyone in the world homosexual. I had thoughts on how this would be going into it, but I'm really glad that the story was lighter than my expectations and more focused on the main couple's friendship and their feelings for one another— and their shared love of Ayumu's late grandfather. I love how Kazusa and Ayumu were friends from childhood - love that trope! - but their relationship was made even better that they had a shared role model in Ayumu's grandfather, who was supposedly one of the last heterosexual people in the world.

The world-building and explanation for everyone's gayness were explained pretty well, and there were reminders throughout the chapters. Not enough to be redundant, but just enough to keep in mind why the world is the way it is and how it got there. While there is a love triangle, it doesn't really start until volume 2, just hinted at in volume 1. It didn't feel overdone, as our Kazusa really only had eyes for one boy, so the triangle was pretty one-sided. [Insert geometry joke here].

The art is really pretty, with exceptional use of screen tones and soft lines. My only gripe is that the ending felt a little flat and left me wondering some things. However, there was a short bonus chapter at the end of the second (and last) volume to clear some things up for the reader, and Kazusa. I'm pretty sure most people who have dated have had that moment at least once.
